longterm_thesis:
One sentence governs the next decade: the scarce goods are electrons, trust and time, and all three are being repriced against a ~5% risk-free rate that is the regime rather than an anomaly. Every brief from 13 Sep to 6 Oct 2026 repeats the same convergence — compute and generation have become a single capital-allocation decision. Google signing a 20-year nuclear PPA with Constellation, Meta funding seven gas plants for one campus, Amazon's $8B Generac order, Mitsui contracting LNG explicitly for data centers, Korea's reported $200bn into US nuclear/LNG, Italy and Poland reversing decades of nuclear policy, ERCOT's 2030s load curve. Generation, fuel cycle, transmission EPC and siting regain pricing power lost for forty years, and the binding constraint on AI has demonstrably moved from silicon to power and permits. Capital is visibly rotating out of housing and rate-sensitive real assets (Kashkari's framing; Real Estate at -91, Utilities flows negative while utility earnings guidance rises — a dislocation, not a verdict) and into the electron supply chain. The implication for capital is that the durable claim on AI is the physical chokepoint, not the model: fuel, firm power, HBM bits, optics, copper, switchgear, skilled trades.

The second compounding line is that delegation creates a new, permanent need: provable containment. Humans are buying AI as time, not intelligence — the fastest-rising consumer queries across six separate briefs are 'ai phone assistant', 'ai phone answering service', 'ai agent builder'; ChatGPT reached ~1bn monthly mobile users. But once a machine acts on your behalf, identity, delegated authority, audit trail and kill-switch become non-discretionary. Nvidia is building that reference architecture in the open (Vera, DigiCert agent identity, Open Agent Safety Platform, 100+ partners) while Washington prefers a voluntary accord and California starts a state patchwork on AI 'robo bosses'. Private standards arrive before regulation, which means security converts from a defensive cost centre into a metered utility on every agent action — the most defensible annuity in the AI stack, and the reason cybersecurity tops flow rankings. Enterprises blocking Anthropic models over data fears is the same behaviour: the cost per unit of AI adoption is structurally rising, and that cost accrues to governance and security vendors, not to model vendors.

The third line is behavioural adaptation to unaffordability. At 7%+ mortgages and a 19-year-high long end, housing need does not resolve — it substitutes. Households renovate instead of relocating (HD/LOW attention +51%/+73.5%, repeatedly flagged 'not priced'), rent longer, live multigenerationally, extend car-loan duration to protect a monthly payment, and fund consumption from paper wealth while confidence sits at a 12-14 year low. Spending bifurcates by income: TJX and Walmart raise guidance, Carnival books record deposits at the top end, Nike has its worst year ever in the squeezed middle. Simultaneously, market structure itself is being unbundled across time (24/7 and tokenized equities, weekend trading), access (SEC retail private-asset proposals, prediction markets) and venue (TXSE at $80-100bn of listings, NSE India, Manila IPOs) — which durably advantages exchanges, brokers and rails over asset gatherers, while quietly pushing illiquidity to households late in a cycle.

Underneath everything sits demography and fiscal arithmetic: Western populations begin shrinking around 2029, debt service exceeds nominal GDP growth, and $365 trillion of global debt means sovereigns compete with corporates at every auction. That makes productivity-per-worker (agents, robotics, healthspan) the only growth lever and term premium a permanent feature. Portfolio consequence: underwrite equities against a 5% risk-free rate, own constraint owners and toll roads with cash conversion, be sceptical of anything whose moat was cheap capital — marginal housing, levered consumers, REIT roll-ups, pre-revenue AI IPOs and vendor-financed neoclouds. The AI drawdown, when it comes, will be a financing event (circular vendor financing, insurer-wrapped GPU loans), not a demand event — which means the physical layer survives it and the capital-structure layer does not.

memo.summary: This is a defensive-value book dressed as a momentum book: 54% net equity (below the 61% recommended and well below the 65% baseline) at a beta of 1.03, with the other 46% spread across 16% cash, 14% Treasuries (IEF/TLT), 6% gold, 5% IG credit and 5% broad commodities. The regime read is a near coin-flip between Reflation (33%) and Stagflation (34%) with inflation momentum +10.1 and liquidity -9.0 over 60 days, and the equity sleeve is positioned for exactly that: cheap, cash-generative, non-duration-sensitive franchises in the two sectors where capital is actually flowing (Health Care rotation 94, Financials 55), funded by a near-complete exit from Technology after HPQ stopped out, CRM was flagged out on brief escalation, and ZBRA fell out of the ranking. Every equity name is a reality-ahead-of-pricing trade — weighted reality 57 vs pricing 46, a 12-point expectations gap — and nine of eleven are in confirmed stage-2 uptrends. The bet, bluntly, is that value keeps leading growth (currently by 123 points), that the Health Care and Financials bid persists, and that the sticky-inflation tilt is handled by the commodity/gold/cash sleeves rather than by the equity selection.

key_bets.why: Highest conviction (31.3) and the only HFE-boosted name at 1.08x. Perfect 100 momentum and 100 technical with zero warnings, 2.3% off 52w highs, margins +612bps YoY, and value score 96. Note the expected-return model is flagged LOW CONFIDENCE and single-method — fair value is >60% above price, so the market is pricing a de-rating the multiples do not capture. We are buying the trend and the margin expansion, not the 76% modelled return.

Best entry score in the book (76) with flows at 97 and the strongest sector tailwind available (Health Care rotation 94). Revenue accelerating to +10.1%, ROIC 32.1%, four valuation methods agreeing. Earnings in 3 days is the near-term swing factor and the thesis explicitly concedes ~1% operating margins and negative equity cap the re-rating.

At a 52-week high, 100 technical, 100 momentum, zero warnings, +111bps margin, +33.7% FCF, buying back ~3% of shares — and still a 12x P/E. Lowest modelled upside of the insurers (base +14.9%) but the cleanest trend.

The weakest technical of the three insurers (75, 'emerging' stage, 50-day declining, RSI 68.5) but value 91 and a post-earnings drift window open for 45 days. Essentially a third expression of the same P&C pricing-cycle trade.

Deepest expectations gap in the book (20 points, pricing 35 vs reality 55) with HC flows at 97, but 12-month return is negative and it lags its sector on both 3m and 6m RS. Earnings in 3 days. This is the highest-variance Health Care position.

Genuine fundamental inflection (revenue +9.1% from +1.1%, FCF +107%) bought against a -29 Industrials rotation score — a deliberate fade of the flow signal. The 8-K officer change applied a 0.9x haircut and conviction is only 10.9.

The weakest hand in the book: catalyst score 40 with zero identified catalysts, three momentum warnings, -12.5% over 3m, margins -2.3pts and incremental ROIC -36%. Held on a LOW-CONFIDENCE valuation and 6.8x P/FCF. Size is at full 5% despite conviction of 10.7 — this is the first position to question.

Strongest relative strength in the portfolio (+62 vs sector over 6m, +60.7 RS) on a 0.6 long-term Edge AI theme conviction, but the lowest conviction score (6.0), 39.1% vol, a 45 valuation score and only 7.2% expected return. Pure trend-following, and the Edge AI theme trend (41) is the closest of any theme to its exit threshold (31).

The only legacy holding, -4.6%, trimmed to 4% on momentum deterioration (half size) and explicitly flagged a swap candidate on ER/vol of 0.70 versus a 4.14 best alternative. No exit rule has triggered, so it stays — but it is on the block.

concentrations: Health Care 23% across four names (CAH, BMY, CI, DXCM) — the single largest sector bet, resting almost entirely on the rotation score holding at 94 and flows at 97.

Three P&C insurers (TRV, CINF, CB) at 15% combined. These are one trade, not three: same pricing cycle, same reserve-release dynamics, same catastrophe exposure. Correlation here is far higher than the position count suggests.
Industrials 15% (FDX, DAL, MAS) bought *against* a -29 sector rotation score — an explicit bet that stock-level fundamentals override the flow signal in a group capital is leaving.
Deep value factor: weighted pricing 46 vs reality 57; value scores of 96, 91, 91, 86, 81, 79. The book is long the value-over-growth spread that is currently 123 points wide.
Event risk cluster: CAH and CI both report in 3 days, 10% of book, both new full-size positions with zero cushion from entry.

Valuation-model fragility: TRV, CINF and CB carry n_methods=1, and TRV, DAL and CI are flagged LOW CONFIDENCE with fair value >60% above price. Roughly 25% of the equity sleeve rests on thin valuation evidence.
Near-zero exposure to Energy and Consumer Staples despite both being named as accelerating-flow sectors, and effectively zero Technology after this week's exits.
biggest_risks: Insurer correlation: a single large catastrophe quarter or a turn in the P&C pricing cycle hits TRV, CINF and CB simultaneously. Their stops sit 5.3-6.1% away, tighter than the book average, so a correlated 7% drawdown exits 15% of the portfolio at once.

Health Care rotation is at 94 — a maximal reading that can only deteriorate. Twenty-three percent of the book is priced off that tailwind persisting, and the exit rule only fires below -30 for two consecutive weeks, which means the system will ride a long way down before the rules act.

The regime exit rule sits at 55% adverse probability and the current reading is 50.9% (Stagflation 34.2 + Contraction 16.7). A two-point move in either direction flips every holding's regime rule simultaneously — a synchronised, book-wide liquidation trigger.
Industrials rotation is -29 against a -30 threshold. One point of further deterioration, sustained two weeks, forces exits in FDX, DAL and MAS together.
DAL has no catalysts, deteriorating momentum on three counts, compressing margins, and is held on a valuation the model itself flags as unreliable. It is a 5% position carried on 10.7 conviction.
The low-confidence valuation flag is a warning, not noise: when the model says fair value is 60%+ above price, the market usually knows something the multiples don't. TRV, DAL and CI all carry it.

Turnover of 35.5% in one week with ten of eleven positions entered at the same price on the same day. There is no diversification of entry timing — a market-wide drawdown next week puts the entire equity sleeve underwater at once with no trailing-stop cushion anywhere.
Being 54% equity against a 61% recommendation and 65% baseline is a meaningful drag if Reflation (33%) resolves to the upside. The sleeve positioning hedges stagflation at the cost of participation.
BBY at 39.1% volatility with the lowest conviction in the book and a theme trend only 10 points above its exit threshold is the most likely source of an idiosyncratic stop-out.
what_would_change_our_mind: Adverse regime probability crossing 55% — that is the system-wide kill switch and it is 4.1 points away.
Health Care rotation rolling over from 94 toward neutral, or the flows read (currently 97 for CAH/CI) deteriorating. That would undercut the single largest sector bet before any exit rule fires.
Financials rotation turning negative for two consecutive weeks, which would invalidate the shared leg of the three-insurer trade and demand we treat them as one position rather than three.
Industrials rotation breaching -30 and holding — forced exit in 15% of the book, and confirmation that fading the flow signal on FDX/DAL/MAS was wrong.

The value-over-growth spread narrowing materially from 123 points, or Technology/Communication Services flows turning from deteriorating to accelerating. The entire equity sleeve is one side of that factor trade.
CAH or CI earnings missing in three days — a gap-down on either would invalidate the revenue-acceleration leg the way HPQ's -9.6% pre-market gap invalidated its thesis this week.
DXCM's ER/vol gap closing versus the 4.14 best alternative, or widening further — the latter should force the swap rather than another week of holding.
Long-duration Treasury flows reversing, which would challenge the 14% duration sleeve that is currently doing part of the defensive work.
memo.hedging_note: The hedge is structural, not tactical: 46% of the book sits outside equities, deliberately built as a stagflation straddle — 16% cash, 14% Treasuries (8.4% IEF / 5.6% TLT, supported by the accelerating long-duration flow signal), 6% gold and 5% commodities to cover the inflation leg, plus 5% IG credit. That is above baseline in Treasuries, cash and gold and at baseline in commodities, consistent with the risk posture of 55 ('Stable') and the beta step-down from 1.1 to 1.03. Equity-level protection is stop-based only: average stop distance 6.7%, with hard stops 10-12% below entry. The weakness is that the stops are all set from the same entry date at the same prices, so they offer no protection against a correlated gap — and the three insurers, with the tightest stops in the book, are the most likely to all fire together. No index or options overlay is in place; the cash sleeve is the drawdown buffer.
watchlist: CNC (Centene) — the only formal candidate: technical score 100 and opportunity 56, but conviction is just 5.3 and the gap only 2. Trigger: a widening expectations gap above ~8 or a conviction move into double digits would make it a cleaner Health Care expression than CI.
DXCM — already flagged a swap candidate at ER/vol 0.70 vs a 4.14 alternative. Trigger: another week of momentum deterioration or a break of the 79.39 stop, at which point replace rather than re-trim.
DAL — trigger: any further loss of the 73.74 stop zone, or a fourth momentum warning. With catalyst score 40 and no scheduled events, there is no reason to wait for the rules.

Energy names — flows are accelerating and we own none. Trigger: any Energy candidate clearing the ranking with a stage-2 technical read; it would also improve the stagflation hedge inside the equity sleeve.
Consumer Staples — same logic as Energy: named as an accelerating-flow sector with zero representation in the book.
BBY — trigger: Edge AI theme trend falling below 31 (currently 41) forces the exit; given 39.1% vol and 6.0 conviction, we would act before the rule fires.

Technology re-entry — Tech rotation is -58 and flows deteriorating. Trigger: two consecutive weeks of improving Tech flows would mark the point to stop treating the sector as uninvestable, particularly given Cybersecurity is leading the sub-theme ranking.
